extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsels, PR practitioners, and students of public relations
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and practical standards for public relations counsel on shaping and communicating with public opinion, including use of media, timing, psychology of crowds/herds, and institutional constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take the public into its confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: “The best way to insure public coöperation was to take the public into its confidence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use open public statements to build trust and cooperation; treat the public as a partner rather than hiding motives. Example: editorials urging public coöperation during conferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public statements as tests (trial balloons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public statements “were used by the diplomats themselves as a happy means of testing popular opinion upon the various projects offered in council.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Float ideas publicly to gauge reaction before committing policy; monitor responses and adjust plans accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain clipping/monitoring bureaus to gauge opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: “Each delegation maintained clipping bureaus, which were brought up to date every morning and which gave the delegates accurate information as to the state of mind at home.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously collect and summarize media coverage and public commentary to stay informed about public sentiment and trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlist the established point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: “The moulder of public opinion must enlist the established point of view.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with prevailing public attitudes and recognized cultural patterns rather than attempting to overturn them immediately; align messages to existing frames where possible. Anti-pattern: ignoring entrenched views and expecting instant conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple channels and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: The Safety First movement used “every form of appeal, from poster to circular, from lecture to law enforcement, from motion pictures to ‘safety weeks’.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a multimodal campaign across print, posters, lectures, film, events and legal measures to change habits and attitudes incrementally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine analysis, applied expertise, and public education
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rockefeller Foundation brought change “by analysis, investigation, applied medical principles, and public education.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pair rigorous research and technical intervention with educational outreach to effect behavioral change and public acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the mirrors of the public mind (media standards & audiences)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Study of the mirrors of the public mind—the press, the motion pictures, the lecture platform and the others—reveal to him what their standards are and those of the groups they reach.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze each medium’s conventions, audience composition and standards to tailor format, tone and content appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire thorough knowledge of group and individual psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: “A fundamental study of group and individual psychology is required before the public relations counsel can determine how readily individuals or groups will accept modifications of viewpoints or policies.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn crowd, herd and individual motivational mechanisms to predict receptivity and design persuasive strategies; do not rely solely on surface demographics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and work with cultural stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes “largely determine what group of facts we shall see and in what light we shall see them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify prevailing stereotypes and cultural frames that shape perception; craft messages that fit or gently reframe those stereotypes rather than contradicting them abruptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand crowd and herd dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowd/herd concepts: the crowd is a state of mind; herd characteristics include homogeneity, intolerance of solitude, susceptibility to leadership, and strong suggestibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for herd tendencies—desire for identification, leadership effects, rationalization of group standards—when planning messages, mobilization, and leadership selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure common ground with the target group's traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The cause he represents must have some group reaction and tradition in common with the public he is trying to reach. This must exist before they can react sympathetically upon one another.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that your advocacy shares roots, symbols, or traditions with the audience; if not, prioritize building shared references before expecting support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect timing and public readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: Madam Curie’s reception depended on prior public apprise­ment; a prison reform talk during a crime wave will find little response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose moments when the public is receptive; campaigns launched at the wrong time (or too early) risk indifference or hostility. Monitor readiness signals before major pushes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage leaders and influencers already aligned with your message
rubrics_metrics.description: “The very ‘leaders’... live with their ears to the ground for every slight rumbling of public sentiment.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partner with established leaders whose audiences already share sympathies; leaders can amplify but cannot create sympathy ex nihilo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand news-selection constraints and placement effects
rubrics_metrics.description: News prominence is affected by “what else happened that day” and the paper’s clientele; selection, position, space and emphasis shape public perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for the news cycle: pick dates, angles, and placements to maximize attention; avoid launching important items on days likely to be overshadowed by major events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize institutional market constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: “The very fact that newspapers must sell to the public is an evidence that they must please the public and in a measure obey it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect media institutions to prioritize content that fits their audience’s tastes and commercial needs. Messaging should accommodate those constraints for effective coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent editorial/organizational stance when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: the two Baltimore Suns “have courageously and consistently stood for the policies of their editors and have refused to yield to pressure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency and bravery in stance can build credibility and long-term influence; weigh risks but avoid flip-flopping in face of pressure when principle and strategy justify steadiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limits: you cannot manufacture public opinion from nothing
rubrics_metrics.description: “The public relations counsel is not needed to persuade people to standardize their points of view... The public relations counsel is not responsible for public opinion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set realistic objectives: PR can intensify, amplify, or nudge opinion where foundations exist, but cannot wholly create durable mass acceptance without preexisting grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tact and avoid careless rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: “He can intensify it, or by tactless speaking he can dissipate it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft language and delivery carefully; tactless remarks can rapidly erode sympathy and undo carefully built rapport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build credibility through accurate, fair, and service-oriented reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The World published truthful series on the Ku Klux Klan and other campaigns, stressing accuracy and fairness so other papers would cooperate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain accuracy and fairness to win co‑operation and credibility; factual, service-oriented campaigns are more likely to be syndicated or supported by peers.
